title: Home and Decoration
description: Ten stories and short texts about making a home: an old brick house, a careful carpenter, choosing paint colors, a balcony garden, a flea-market portrait, a tiny apartment, a ramp for a grandfather, a designer's simulation, a church turned into a home and a mountain cabin.

lessons.title: The Brick House on Lincoln Street
lessons.summary: Ellen and Mark buy an old brick house, consult an engineer, strengthen the kitchen floor and slowly bring the house back to life.
lessons.text:
When Ellen and Mark first saw the house on Lincoln Street, it was a gray October afternoon, and the old building looked tired. It was a two-story brick house, built in 1912, with tall windows and a wide front door. Its red bricks had turned dark with age. Inside, the air smelled of dust and cigarette smoke, because the last owner had smoked in every room for 40 years.

Mark wanted to leave after five minutes. Ellen, however, stood in the empty living room and watched the soft light falling across the floor. "This house could be beautiful again," she said. "It just needs someone to care about it."

Before they made an offer, they decided to consult an engineer. A house that old could potentially hide serious problems, and they did not want to spend their savings on a building that was not safe. The engineer, a calm woman named Diane Ruiz, spent a whole morning in the basement.

Her report was clear. The brick walls were strong, and the roof was in good condition. However, one of the main supports under the kitchen floor was under strain. For many years a heavy iron stove had stood above it, and the strain had slowly bent the wood. "It isn't dangerous yet," Diane explained, "but it is potentially dangerous. You will need to strengthen it before you do anything else."

She added that the problem did not warrant panic; it warranted a careful plan. A builder could strengthen the support with a steel plate in two or three days. "A strong floor is vital," she said. "Paint and new cabinets can wait. This can't."

Ellen and Mark bought the house in November. Since a strong floor was vital, they consulted a builder about it first, and within a week the old support was no longer under any strain. In the subsequent weeks, they opened every window, washed every wall and slowly removed the smell of cigarettes. It took three washings before the rooms stopped smelling of old cigarette smoke.

The subsequent months were full of small jobs. They repaired the front steps, cleaned the bricks around the door and painted the bedrooms a soft blue. Each job was simple, but together they changed the house. By spring, the brick house on Lincoln Street no longer looked tired.

One evening Mark stood in the living room, exactly where Ellen had stood months before. "You were right," he said. "It just needed someone to care about it."

Questions:
Why did the house smell of cigarette smoke?
It smelled of cigarette smoke because the last owner had smoked in every room for 40 years.
Why did Ellen and Mark consult an engineer?
They consulted an engineer because a house that old could potentially hide serious problems.
What was under strain?
One of the main supports under the kitchen floor was under strain.
How could a builder strengthen the support?
A builder could strengthen it with a steel plate in two or three days.
Did the problem warrant panic?
No, it did not warrant panic, but it warranted a careful plan.
What did Ellen and Mark do in the subsequent months?
They repaired the front steps, cleaned the bricks and painted the bedrooms.

lessons.title: The Carpenter
lessons.summary: A mature carpenter repairs the scratched floor of the narrator's apartment and teaches the narrator to see the history in old wood.
lessons.text:
Last spring I bought a small apartment in an old building, and the first thing I noticed was the floor. It was made of wide wood boards, but it was covered in scratches. Some scratches were long and deep; others were as fine as a hair. My neighbor gave me the number of a carpenter called Sam Porter, who, she said, had repaired half the floors on our street.

Sam arrived on a Monday morning. He was a mature man of about 60, with gray hair, strong hands and a small tattoo of a tree on his left arm. When he noticed me looking at the tattoo, he smiled. "I got it when I was 19," he said. "My father was a carpenter too, and the tree is for him."

He walked slowly through the apartment and occasionally stopped to touch a scratch with his finger. He had a remark for every room. In the kitchen he remarked that the boards were older than the building itself. In the bedroom he remarked that someone had once repaired them badly. I found it incredibly interesting. I had always thought of a floor as something you walk on, not something with a history.

"Most of these scratches will go away when I sand the floor," he explained. "The deep ones will stay, but they will become part of its character. An old floor is like a mature person. It shouldn't pretend to be young."

For four days the apartment was full of noise and fine dust. Sam worked incredibly carefully. He cared equally about the corners and the middle of the room, and he treated the old boards and the newer ones equally. Occasionally he stopped for coffee and told me about other old houses.

On the third day I mentioned that the pole above my bedroom window was falling down. It held my curtains, and it had been loose since I moved in. Sam looked at the pole and shook his head. "Whoever put this up used the wrong screws," he said. He fixed the pole in ten minutes and refused to take any money for it.

When the floor was finished, it shone with a warm golden color. A few deep scratches were still there, exactly as he had said, and I liked them. Before he left, Sam offered to lend me some of his tools. "Everyone should own good tools," he said, "but until you buy your own, I'm happy to lend you mine." I still have them.

Questions:
What was the floor covered in?
It was covered in scratches, some long and deep, others very fine.
What did Sam's tattoo show, and why did he get it?
It showed a tree, and he got it for his father, who was also a carpenter.
What did Sam remark in the kitchen?
He remarked that the boards were older than the building itself.
Why did Sam say an old floor is like a mature person?
He said it because an old floor, like a mature person, shouldn't pretend to be young.
What was wrong with the pole above the bedroom window?
It was falling down because someone had used the wrong screws.
What did Sam offer to lend the narrator?
He offered to lend the narrator some of his tools.

lessons.title: The Color of a Room
lessons.summary: A columnist learns why a paint color changes between the store and the wall, and how to choose one that suits a room.
lessons.text:
The Color of a Room
By Nora Bell

Every few years I decide to paint a room, and every time I make the same mistake. In the paint store, I choose a color that looks lovely on a small card under the bright lights, and I take it home. Then, on my own wall, the color turns into something else entirely.

This time I wanted to understand why. A friend who works in a paint shop explained a little of the chemistry behind it. Paint is made of many materials, and the chemistry of each color is slightly different. Some paints contain a high concentration of color, which makes them look intense. An intense red or blue is wonderful on a card, but on four walls it can feel heavy. Hence the advice that painters commonly give: choose a shade one or two steps lighter than the one you love.

Light matters too. A color that looks warm in the morning can look cold in the evening. My friend made a simple observation that I have not forgotten: "People choose colors in the store, but they live with them at home."

So this time I painted three large squares of different colors on my living room wall and left them there for a week. Each day I wrote down a short observation: how each square looked at breakfast, at lunch and after dark. The variation surprised me. A soft green that seemed calm in the middle of the day turned almost gray at night. A warm yellow, on the other hand, changed very little; its variation from morning to evening was hardly visible.

I also noticed that old marks on the wall were still visible under a single layer of light paint. Hence, as people commonly say, two layers are better than one.

Increasingly, paint stores let customers take home large sample sheets instead of tiny cards. Increasingly, too, people choose softer colors for bedrooms and keep intense colors for a single wall or a front door. A deep blue is said to help concentration, which may be why it is popular for home offices.

In the end, no color is suitable for every room. I chose the warm yellow. It is not the most exciting color in the store, but it is suitable for a room where I read, eat and talk with friends, and it looks almost the same from morning until night.

Questions:
Why can some paints look intense?
They can look intense because they contain a high concentration of color.
What observation did Nora's friend make?
She said that people choose colors in the store, but they live with them at home.
What did Nora notice about the soft green?
She noticed that it seemed calm in the middle of the day but turned almost gray at night.
Why are two layers of paint better than one?
They are better because old marks are still visible under a single layer of light paint.
Why did Nora choose the warm yellow?
She chose it because it is suitable for a room where she reads, eats and talks with friends, and it hardly changes during the day.

lessons.title: A Garden on the Sixth Floor
lessons.summary: Rosa turns the bare balcony of her sixth-floor apartment into a small garden full of peppers.
lessons.text:
Rosa lives on the sixth floor of an apartment building in the middle of the city. From her balcony she can see roofs, a few trees and, on a clear day, the river. For years the balcony held nothing but a chair and an old bike. Last March, Rosa decided to turn it into a garden.

She knew nothing about agriculture. To her, agriculture meant wide fields and large machines, not a small concrete space on the sixth floor. Still, she read a few books about growing food in small spaces and learned that city agriculture is increasingly popular all over the world.

She started with 8 large pots, a few bags of soil and some young plants. Most of them were peppers. One kind would give sweet red peppers, another small, hot green ones, and the pepper plants quickly became the ones she loved most.

The man at the garden shop gave her an important piece of advice. "Every pot needs holes in the bottom, so that the water can drain," he said. "If the water can't drain, the roots will die."

Every evening, a long green hose snaked across her living room floor from the kitchen to the plants. To keep the birds away from the young leaves, she placed a toy snake among the pots. The birds did not like the snake at all, and they soon found another place to visit.

In June, tiny green insects appeared on the peppers. Rosa did not want to use poison, because she planned to eat the peppers and because poison might also harm the bees. Instead, she mixed water with a little soap until small bubbles formed, and she sprayed the leaves with it every few days. When the bubbles dried, most of the insects were gone.

The bees were her quiet friends. A man on the top floor kept two boxes of bees on the roof, and Rosa liked to think that her pepper flowers helped to make his honey. In September he knocked on her door with a jar of golden honey as a thank-you.

Rosa also learned to save water. When she boiled potatoes or eggs, she let the water cool and gave it to her plants. In October, she wrapped the pots in bubble wrap to protect the roots from the cold nights. That evening she cooked dinner with her own peppers, put her neighbor's honey in her tea and sat outside until it was dark.

Questions:
Where does Rosa live?
She lives on the sixth floor of an apartment building in the middle of the city.
What did agriculture mean to Rosa before?
To her, agriculture meant wide fields and large machines.
Why does every pot need holes in the bottom?
It needs holes so that the water can drain.
Why did Rosa place a toy snake among the pots?
She placed it there to keep the birds away from the young leaves.
Why did Rosa not want to use poison?
She did not want to use poison because she planned to eat the peppers and because it might harm the bees.
What did Rosa do with the water she used to boil potatoes or eggs?
She let it cool and gave it to her plants.

lessons.title: The Woman in the Blue Dress
lessons.summary: At a Sunday flea market, Daniel buys an old portrait of a woman in a blue dress and learns its story.
lessons.text:
That Sunday, Daniel Kim had planned to go cycling with a friend, but the friend canceled at the last minute. Daniel did not feel like staying at home, so he walked to the flea market behind the old train station instead.

The market was busy, even in the light rain. Two rival sellers had their tables side by side, and they were offering lower and lower prices for almost the same wood chairs. The two rivals seemed to enjoy the game as much as their customers did. Nearby, a woman sold baskets made by a Native American tribe, and she told every customer the name of the tribe and of the woman who had made each basket.

Then Daniel saw the portrait. It was a painting of a young woman in a blue dress, sitting by a window with her hands in her lap. She was not smiling, but her eyes looked kind. Daniel wondered how many hours she had posed for the artist, sitting still in that same position. The portrait was small, and its frame was damaged, but he could not stop looking at it.

"How much is it?" he asked.

"It's 40 dollars," said the owner of the table, an older man named Mr. Grant. "It came from a house on Hill Road. The family didn't know who the artist was."

Daniel bought it. On the way home he wondered whether he had found a fortune. In films, people find a lost painting at a market and make a fortune. On the other hand, he had read that some people commit fraud by selling cheap copies as old paintings.

So he took the portrait to his friend Ana, who works at the city museum. Ana studied it carefully. "It isn't worth a fortune," she said, "but it isn't a fraud either. It's a real oil painting, about 100 years old, and it's quite well done."

"Who was she, do you think?" Daniel asked.

"That's a valid question," said Ana, "but I can't give you a valid answer. Perhaps she posed for her husband, or for a friend who liked to paint. We may never know."

Daniel repaired the frame and hung the portrait in his living room. He thinks of it as a small legacy: the legacy of an unknown artist and of the woman who once posed for him. He is still glad his friend canceled that Sunday.

Questions:
Why did Daniel go to the flea market?
He went because his friend canceled their plans to go cycling.
What were the two rival sellers doing?
They were offering lower and lower prices for almost the same wood chairs.
What did the woman with the baskets tell her customers?
She told them the name of the tribe and of the woman who had made each basket.
What did the portrait show?
It showed a young woman in a blue dress, sitting by a window with her hands in her lap.
What did Ana say about the portrait?
She said it was not worth a fortune but not a fraud either, because it was a real oil painting about 100 years old.
How does Daniel think of the portrait?
He thinks of it as a small legacy of an unknown artist and of the woman who posed for him.

lessons.title: 300 Square Feet
lessons.summary: In an email to her mother, Lily describes how she made her tiny studio apartment comfortable.
lessons.text:
Hi Mom,

You asked for a full report on the new apartment, so here it is. It's small, as you know: 300 square feet, one main room, a tiny kitchen and a bathroom. It's on a quiet street just behind the bus terminal, so I can walk to the terminal in four minutes and be at work in twenty. After two years of long drives, that feels like real luxury.

At first the room felt like a box. I slept, ate and worked in the same space. So I decided to divide the room into three parts. A tall set of open shelves now divides the bed from the rest of the room, and a big plant divides my "office" from my "living room." The shelves and the plant let the light through, so nothing feels dark.

For the first few weeks I felt a little isolated. I didn't know anyone in the building, and I spent most evenings alone. That has changed, though. My neighbor, Mrs. Lopez, invited me for tea, and now we take turns cooking dinner on Fridays, so I don't feel isolated anymore.

Of course, everything in a small home is a compromise. I wanted a large sofa, but it would have filled half the room, so I chose a narrow one that opens into a guest bed. That compromise means you can come and stay! Another compromise was my clothes. There is only one small closet, so I kept enough outfits for about two weeks and gave the rest away. Honestly, choosing an outfit in the morning is much easier now.

Do you remember your mother's little makeup table? It's here, and it works as my desk. The mirror is still on it, so I do my makeup and answer my emails in the same place. Each apartment also has an assigned storage space in the basement, where I keep my bike. I even have an assigned spot in the parking lot, although I hardly use the car.

I also made a small fitness corner by the window, with a mat and two light weights. It isn't a gym, but it's enough for my fitness routine on rainy mornings. Finally, I bought a long, narrow runner for the floor between the door and the kitchen. The runner is red and yellow, and it makes the whole room look warmer.

My one true luxury is the window seat, where I drink my coffee and watch the buses leave the terminal. Come and see it soon!

Love,
Lily

Questions:
Why does Lily call her short trip to work a luxury?
She calls it a luxury because she can walk to the terminal in four minutes after two years of long drives.
How did Lily divide the room?
She divided it with a tall set of open shelves and a big plant.
Why doesn't Lily feel isolated anymore?
She doesn't feel isolated because her neighbor invited her for tea and now they cook dinner together on Fridays.
What compromise did Lily make about the sofa?
She chose a narrow sofa that opens into a guest bed instead of a large one.
What does Lily use as her desk?
She uses her grandmother's old makeup table as her desk.

lessons.title: A Ramp for Grandpa
lessons.summary: After a fall, Walter, a retired park ranger, moves in with his daughter, and together they remove the barriers in her house.
lessons.text:
For 35 years, Walter Hayes worked as a park ranger in the mountains of Montana. He knew every trail, every river and every kind of bird in the park. Last winter, however, Walter fell on the ice and badly hurt his hip. After the operation, the doctors told him that he would have a disability for the rest of his life. He could walk short distances with a stick, but on most days he would need a wheelchair.

His daughter Karen asked him to move in with her family. Walter did not like the idea. "I've taken care of myself for 80 years," he said. "I'm not going to be a problem for anyone."

Karen did not argue. She understood why her father was defensive. A disability can feel like a loss of freedom, and Walter had always been an active man. Instead, she suggested an open dialogue: every Sunday they would sit down together and talk honestly about what was working and what was not. Slowly, the dialogue helped. Walter became less defensive, and he finally agreed to come.

Karen's house, however, was full of barriers. There were three steps at the front door, the bathroom door was too narrow for a wheelchair, and the kitchen cupboards were too high. A specialist from the hospital, Ms. Grant, came to give her advice. "With respect, Mr. Hayes," she said, "small changes can remove most of these barriers. I would recommend a ramp at the front door and a wider bathroom door."

"Call me Walter," he said. "And go ahead. Let's take down the barriers."

The work took six weeks. Karen's husband built a wood ramp, and a builder made the bathroom door wider. Karen moved the plates and cups to lower cupboards. Every decision was made after careful consideration, and with consideration for Walter's pride. He chose the color of the ramp himself: forest green.

Of course, small problems continued to arise. Whenever one arose, such as a chair that blocked the hall, they talked about it on Sunday and found a solution.

In the evenings, Walter often watched nature documentaries. One documentary was about the park where he had worked, and he told the whole family which trails the film crew had used. That gave Karen an idea. She found a bird club for older people, and in April Walter resumed his old hobby of watching birds. Now, every Thursday morning, he sits by the river with the club and watches the birds, and he says he feels like a ranger again.

Questions:
What was Walter's job for 35 years?
He worked as a park ranger in the mountains of Montana.
Why was Walter defensive at first?
He was defensive because his disability felt like a loss of freedom, and he did not want to be a problem for anyone.
What kind of dialogue did Karen suggest?
She suggested an open dialogue every Sunday about what was working and what was not.
What barriers were in the house?
There were three steps at the front door, a narrow bathroom door and high kitchen cupboards.
What did the family do when small problems arose?
They talked about them on Sunday and found a solution.
Which hobby did Walter resume?
He resumed his old hobby of watching birds.

lessons.title: The Room Inside the Screen
lessons.summary: An interior designer scans a couple's living room and shows them a computer simulation of her plan before any work begins.
lessons.text:
Priya Shah is an interior designer. She studied design abroad, first in Italy and then in Denmark, and after six years abroad she came home and opened a small studio. Most of her clients are families who want to improve one or two rooms without moving.

One of those families was Tom and Julia Morgan. They had lived in their apartment for ten years, and they no longer liked their living room. It was dark, crowded and loud. On her first visit, Priya did not bring paint cards or furniture books. She brought a tablet.

"With your permission," she said, "I will scan the room first." She walked slowly around the walls, holding the tablet in front of her. In less than ten minutes, the scan was complete, and the program could measure every wall, window and door from it. Tom was surprised. "I didn't know a tablet had that capability," he said. "Most of them do now," Priya answered. "The real capability is in the program."

A week later she came back to give a presentation of her plan. The presentation was short and clear. First, she showed them a simulation of their living room as it was: dark brown walls, a huge sofa, heavy curtains. Then she showed a second simulation with her changes. In it, the walls were light gray, the sofa was smaller, and the curtains were thin and soft. Julia could "walk" through the room on the screen and look at it from every corner.

Both Morgans were quite vocal about their wishes. Tom was vocal about keeping his large television. Julia was equally vocal about wanting more light and a place to read. Priya listened carefully and found a way to give each of them what they wanted.

Then she raised the problem of noise. "The wall you share with the next apartment is quite thin," she said. "I would suggest tall shelves of books along that wall. Books are excellent at reducing the transmission of sound." She showed them on the screen how the transmission of noise through the wall would fall.

"Isn't that a big job?" Julia asked.

"Not at all," said Priya. "I prefer a light intervention. The best intervention is often the smallest one that solves the problem."

The work took three weeks. When it was finished, Julia stood in the middle of the room and laughed. It looked exactly like the simulation, only warmer, and it was much quieter than before.

Questions:
Where did Priya study design?
She studied design abroad, first in Italy and then in Denmark.
Why did Priya scan the room?
She scanned it so that the program could measure every wall, window and door.
What did Priya show in her presentation?
She showed a simulation of the room as it was and a second simulation with her changes.
What were Tom and Julia vocal about?
Tom was vocal about keeping his television, and Julia was vocal about wanting more light and a place to read.
How can books help with noise?
Books are excellent at reducing the transmission of sound through a wall.
What kind of intervention does Priya prefer?
She prefers a light intervention, the smallest one that solves the problem.

lessons.title: From Church to Home
lessons.summary: A short local news report about an old church that residents saved and a couple turned into a family home.
lessons.text:
A New Life for the Stone Church on Mill Road

For more than a hundred years, the small stone church on Mill Road was a place of worship for the farming families of Millbrook. It was built in 1889, with thick walls, a tall wood door and six narrow windows, each with a pointed arch at the top. In its days of glory, its old organ could be heard all along the street on Sunday mornings. However, as the town grew older and smaller, fewer people came to worship there, and in 2015 the last service was held.

For several years the building stood empty. Then, in 2020, a company asked the city for permission to tear it down and build a fast-food restaurant, part of a national franchise. Many residents did not want another franchise on Mill Road. They wanted to keep the church, even if it could no longer be a place of worship.

A group of residents started a petition. In two months, more than 2,000 people signed the petition, which asked the city council to protect the building. According to the town charter, a historic building cannot be removed until the council has held a public meeting. At that meeting, many residents spoke, and the council decided to protect the church. The franchise found another location on the edge of town.

In 2022 the church was bought by Paul and Helen Ward, a couple with two children. Turning an old church into a home was not simple. The city found several violations of the modern building code, including old electrical wiring and no proper fire exit. Every violation had to be fixed before the family could move in.

The Wards decided to change as little as possible. The six arched windows are still there, and under the highest arch there is now a long kitchen table. The old organ remains in the living room, and Paul, who played the organ as a boy, is slowly learning to play it again. A local artist helped to bring the painted walls back to their former glory.

"We don't really feel like owners," says Paul. "We feel more like guardians. The building was here long before us, and it will be here long after us. A guardian's job is to take care of it." This summer, the family invited everyone who had signed the petition to a concert in their home. For one evening, the old church was full again.

Questions:
What was the stone church until 2015?
It was a place of worship for the farming families of Millbrook.
Why did many residents not want the restaurant?
They did not want another franchise on Mill Road, and they wanted to keep the church.
What did the petition ask the city council to do?
It asked the city council to protect the building.
What does the town charter say about historic buildings?
It says that a historic building cannot be removed until the council has held a public meeting.
What violations did the city find?
It found old electrical wiring and no proper fire exit.
Why do Paul and Helen feel like guardians rather than owners?
They feel like guardians because the building was there long before them and will be there long after them.

lessons.title: The Cabin in the Snow
lessons.summary: The Novak family spends a weekend getting their old mountain cabin ready for the ski season.
lessons.text:
For 30 years, the Novak family's small cabin in the mountains has been their favorite winter destination. It stands at the end of a narrow road, half an hour from the nearest ski area, with tall trees on three sides and a view of the valley on the fourth. Every December, before the ski season begins, the family drives up for a weekend to get the cabin ready.

This year Anna Novak went with her husband Peter and their two children, Ella, who is seven, and Leo, who is nine. When they arrived, the cabin was cold and quiet, and snow covered the front steps. The first job was the old iron stove in the corner. It was a black, heavy beast that Anna's family had bought in 1965. It took twenty minutes to light, and it filled the room with smoke before it began to work, but once it was burning, the old beast kept the whole cabin warm all night.

While Peter cleaned the stove, Anna gave the children a job. "I need you two to clean the little room at the back," she said. "Take everything out, sweep the floor and put it all back."

Leo was not happy. "Is this a punishment?"

"It isn't a punishment," Anna laughed. "It's a family cabin, so everyone helps."

"Okay, Mama," said Ella, and she ran to the back room.

An hour later the children came back, very excited. They were carrying a large wood box full of old costumes: a long red coat, a silver crown and a pig mask with pink ears. "Mama, look what we found!" Ella said.

Anna smiled. "Those were your great-grandmother's costumes. She acted in the town theater for many years, and she kept her favorite costumes here."

Leo put on the pig mask at once. "Daddy, do I look like a real pig?" he asked.

"Yep," said Peter, laughing. "You look just like the pigs on the farm down the road."

The rest of the weekend was full of work. Peter fixed a window, and the children helped to carry wood for the stove. In the evenings, nobody worked. They sat around the warm old beast, ate soup and played games, and Ella and Leo wore a different costume each night.

On Sunday afternoon the cabin was clean, warm and ready. "Can we come back for the ski week?" Leo asked.

"Yep," said Ella. "Daddy already said yes."

Questions:
Why is the cabin a good winter destination?
It is a good destination because it is half an hour from the nearest ski area and has a view of the valley.
Why is the stove called a beast?
It is called a beast because it is black and heavy, takes a long time to light and fills the room with smoke.
Why did Leo ask whether the job was a punishment?
He asked because he did not want to clean the little room at the back.
What did the children find in the back room?
They found a large wood box full of old costumes.
Whose costumes were they?
They belonged to the children's great-grandmother, who acted in the town theater.
What did Leo ask his daddy when he put on the pig mask?
He asked if he looked like a real pig.
